title: Scaling Your Portfolio: Refinancing, HELOCs & Property #2

slides.title: Property two starts with proof that property one works
slides.subtitle: Lesson OP.11. Scaling Your Portfolio: Refinancing, HELOCs & Property #2
meta: Education only. Not legal, tax, lending, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
This lesson is about buying a second property. But we're not going to open a single listing. We're going to open the books on the first one.

If property one earned about what you forecast, a second similar house repeats a plan you've already tested. If it didn't, a second house doubles a plan that hasn't worked yet, and it adds a second loan.

By the end of this lesson you'll do three things. You'll build a trailing-12-month report and set it beside your original underwriting. You'll price a cash-out refinance and a home equity line of credit in dollars per month, including a weak year. And you'll write a pass rule for property two and apply it.

What you walk away with is a dated yes, not yet, or no, with the numbers that produced it. We'll use Cedar Ridge at the end of year 2. Everything here is education only. Your lender, CPA, and insurer confirm the real answers.

slides.title: Property two repeats a tested plan only if property one earned what you forecast

left.head: Job one: proof
left.note: What did property one actually do?
items: Actual revenue, from platform earnings reports
Actual costs, from the property's own account and card
Cash left after both
Your original underwriting was a forecast. Twelve months of records are evidence.

right.head: Job two: liquidity
right.note: Where does the cash for property two come from?
items: Savings
A cash-out refinance of property one
A line of credit on your own home
Borrowed money needs a wider margin than savings

slides.notes:
Most people start the property-two conversation with a listing. I want you to start it with a bank statement.

There are two jobs here. The first is proof. You need to know what property one actually earned, what it actually cost, and how much cash is left after both. The underwriting you did with Sam in PA.4 was a forecast. Twelve months of operating records are evidence. This lesson is about reading the evidence before you commit more money.

The second job is liquidity. Buying property two usually means pulling cash from somewhere. That's savings, a refinance of property one, or a loan against the house you live in. Each of those changes your monthly obligations and what you can survive in a weak year.

Keep one rule in mind for the rest of the lesson. A second property funded with borrowed money needs a wider margin than one funded with savings.

slides.title: Build the trailing 12 months from records, starting from Sam's OP.10 review
items: Bring Sam's OP.10 review. It sets your categories and how you pull the data.
Payouts and fees: each booking platform's earnings reports.
Expenses: the property's own bank account and card.
Nights, stays, and nightly rate: property management software (PMS) or calendar.
Three columns: the underwriting you bought on, the actual 12 months, the variance.
If property one's books mix in personal spending, fix that first.
slides.notes:
Sam's OP.10 lesson walks you through the 30-day and 90-day review. Bring that report here. It gives you the categories you track and the way you pull the data. The trailing 12 is the same review stretched to a full year, so every season shows up in it.

Build it from records, not memory. Payouts and fees come from each platform's earnings reports. Expenses come from the property's bank account and card. Booked nights, stays, and your average nightly rate come from your property management software or the platform calendar.

Then set it up in three columns. Column one is the underwriting you bought on. Column two is the actual trailing 12 months. Column three is the variance between them.

One warning. If your bookkeeping mixes property one with personal spending, fix that before you do anything else. The trailing 12 is only as clean as the account behind it.

slides.title: Four checks explain the gap between your underwriting and the actual year
rows: Split it into rate and occupancy
Rate: pricing settings, competition. Occupancy: calendar gaps, minimum stays, reviews, demand
One large repair may be a one-off. A pattern is a budget problem
Did the 5% of gross actually leave the operating account?
If it got spent, cash flow looks better than it is
P&I stays put on a fixed rate. Escrows can change; keep tax and insurance in operating costs

box.label: Plain words
box.text: **NOI** (net operating income) is revenue minus operating costs. **Cash flow** is NOI minus debt service.

slides.notes:
Once you have the variance column, you're looking for four things.

First, split any revenue miss into rate and occupancy. A rate problem often traces to pricing settings or competition. An occupancy problem can trace to calendar gaps, minimum stays, reviews, or demand. Sam's OP.5 lesson covers the pricing tools. Here you only need to know which lever moved.

Second, find the expense lines that grew. One large repair in the year may be a one-off. A pattern of repairs is a budget problem.

Third, check whether you actually funded the capital reserve. If that 5% stayed in the operating account and got spent, your cash flow looks better than it is.

Fourth, compare debt service. Principal and interest, P&I, stay put on a fixed-rate loan. Your lender may also collect tax and insurance through escrow, a monthly add-on it pays for you. Those amounts can change. In the worksheet, keep tax and insurance in operating costs and debt service as P&I only.

The number that matters most is NOI. If trailing NOI is well under your base case, property two waits until you know why. Your pass rule sets what well under means.

slides.title: A cash-out refinance is a new, bigger loan, priced in five steps from a written quote
items: New loan = appraised value × maximum loan-to-value (LTV), the loan as a share of value.
Equity removed = new loan - current loan balance.
Cash out = equity removed - refinance closing costs.
New payment = principal and interest on the new loan at the new rate and term.
New cash flow = NOI - new annual principal and interest.

box.label: Watch three things
box.text: The 30-year clock restarts. Closing costs can eat a large share of a small cash-out. A bigger loan makes a weak year worse, so run weak-case NOI too.

slides.notes:
A cash-out refinance can feel like free money from appreciation. In practice you're replacing your loan with a bigger one, with a new payment, a new term, and new closing costs.

Walk through the math in this order, every time. New loan, equity removed, cash out, new payment, new cash flow.

Every input comes from a written lender quote, not a rule of thumb. The appraisal may come in lower than your estimate. The lender may cap loan-to-value lower than you expect for a short-term rental. It may also apply its own coverage ratio. That's how many dollars of property income it counts for each dollar of loan payment, and PA.6 showed three ways to compute it. Compare quotes the way PA.7 taught, using the CFPB's guide to comparing Loan Estimates where the lender issues one.

Then watch three things. The payoff schedule restarts, and early payments are mostly interest. Closing costs can eat a big share when the equity you remove is small. And because the loan is bigger, a weak year gets worse.

slides.title: A HELOC is secured by your own home, and the lender can freeze it when you need it

left.head: How it works (CFPB)
items: A revolving line secured by a home you own, usually your primary residence
A draw period (10 years in the CFPB example), then repayment
At the end of the draw you may repay over time or owe it all at once, depending on the plan
A variable rate tied to a public index, like prime

right.head: Two risks in plain words
items: Your home is the collateral. If you can't repay, you could lose it.
The lender can generally freeze or cut the line if your home's value drops significantly or your finances change materially.

box.label: Do not do this
box.text: Don't count undrawn HELOC capacity as a reserve. A market dip can remove it at the worst time.

slides.notes:
A home equity line of credit is a revolving line secured by a home you already own. For most people that's the house they live in.

The CFPB describes two phases. During the draw period, and they use 10 years as an example, you can borrow up to your limit. Many plans base the minimum payment on the balance. When the draw period ends, repayment starts. Depending on the plan, you may repay over time or owe the whole balance at once. The rate is usually variable, so price it at today's rate and at a higher stress rate. Read the lender's disclosures before you model anything.

Now the two risks. Your home is the collateral. And the lender can generally freeze or cut the line if your home's value drops significantly or your finances change materially.

There's also a tax question for your CPA. IRS Publication 936 limits the mortgage interest deduction when the money doesn't buy, build, or substantially improve the home securing it. A rental down payment doesn't meet that test. Don't assume either answer in your model.

slides.title: A second house in the same market shares your team but stacks your risk

left.head: Same market
items: The same cleaner, handyman, and supply run may cover both
You already know the permits, seasons, and guests
Reuse your OP.8 playbook with small edits
One bad season, ordinance, or storm hits both houses

right.head: New market
items: Spreads that risk across two places
Needs a new market check (Sam's PA.2) and address review (SR.1)
Needs a new local team and vendor backups
Property one's first-year results don't transfer

slides.notes:
Once the numbers work, the operating question starts. Can your team run two properties as well as it runs one?

A second house in the same market shares a lot. The same cleaner, handyman, and supply run might cover both. You already know the permit process, the seasons, and the guest profile. You can reuse your OP.8 playbook with small edits. The cost is concentration. One bad season, one new ordinance, or one storm now hits both houses at once.

A new market spreads that risk. But the learning curve starts over. You'll need a fresh market check using Sam's PA.2 lesson and a new address-level permission review with resource SR.1. You'll also need a new local team and new vendor backups.

And your first-year results from property one don't tell you much about a market you've never operated in. Treat a new market like a first property on the operating side.

slides.title: Name a primary and a backup for every OP.7 role before you buy property two
slides.text: Roles: write who covers each one at property two and who backs them up.
items: Turnover cleaner
Backup cleaner
Handyman
Emergency contact
Guest messaging
Inspections
Bookkeeping
Supplies
slides.notes:
Whichever market you pick, test your team against the OP.7 role list. Turnover cleaner, backup cleaner, handyman, emergency contact, guest messaging, inspections, bookkeeping, and supplies. For each role, write down who covers it at property two and who backs them up.

Take a simple case. One cleaner covers both houses, and both houses have Saturday turnovers. Unless one person can finish both turnovers in the same checkout window, you likely need a second cleaner before you buy.

The box shows the systems that work across properties. One bookkeeping file with a tag for each property. One calendar view. One set of guest-message templates with the property details filled in. One reserve policy.

If a co-host helps you, give them the least access they need. Airbnb lets you set co-host permission levels, and the listing owner stays responsible for what a co-host does.

box.label: Systems across both houses
box.text: **Systems across both houses:** one bookkeeping file tagged by property, one calendar view, one message template set, one reserve policy, and least-access co-host settings.

slides.title: Cedar Ridge's actual year 2 came in $6,594 under the underwritten NOI
rows: Other costs (handyman, supplies, software, tax, insurance)
slides.caption: Trailing 12: ADR $289, 55% occupancy, 201 nights, 57 stays. Gross includes guest cleaning fees.
slides.notes:
Here's Cedar Ridge at the end of year 2. Maya and Chris are the example couple in this course. They bought it for $385,000 with a DSCR loan at 7.25%. DSCR means debt service coverage ratio: the lender sized the loan mostly on the property's income. Now they're thinking about a second lake-market house.

The first column is their original plan. The trailing 12 is a hypothetical year I built for teaching.

The average daily rate came in at $289 with 55% occupancy: 201 booked nights and 57 stays. Gross also includes the $175 cleaning fee on each stay. So $58,089 of nightly revenue plus $9,975 of cleaning fees gives $68,064, which is $6,211 under plan.

The platform fee and cleaner pay fell with revenue. Repairs jumped $1,486, including a water heater. Net of everything, costs rose only $383. NOI came in at $22,615, and cash flow was minus $1,022.

One cost isn't in these lines: a $400 permit renewal from PA.9. With it, cash flow is minus $1,422. No test result changes.
slides.text: Trailing 12: ADR $289, 55% occupancy, 201 nights, 57 stays. Gross also includes guest cleaning fees.

slides.title: Revenue fell $6,211 and costs rose $383, so a planned $5,572 became -$1,022
slides.side:
Revenue came in at 91.6% of plan. NOI came in at 77.4%. An **8.4% revenue miss became a 22.6% NOI miss**.

The rate was $11 below the $300 planned. Occupancy was 3 points below the 58% planned. Most costs stayed put.

side_box.label: An honest number
side_box.text: The capital reserve was funded, so the -$1,022 isn't flattered by skipped savings.

slides.notes:
This walk shows why a small revenue miss matters so much.

Revenue came in at 91.6% of underwriting. The rate was $11 below the $300 planned, and occupancy was 3 points below 58%. That's an 8.4% miss. But NOI came in at 77.4% of plan, which is a 22.6% miss. Why does it grow? Most costs stay put when revenue drops. Insurance, property tax, software, the handyman retainer, utilities. They don't shrink because you booked fewer nights. So the miss gets bigger on the way down.

Start from the planned cash flow of $5,572. Take away the $6,211 revenue shortfall and the $383 net cost change, and you land at minus $1,022.

One good thing here: they funded the capital reserve. That means minus $1,022 is the honest number, not a flattering one.

If the water heater was a one-off, next year's repairs may fall back toward $3,714. But before they count on a better year, they need to know why rate and occupancy slipped.

slides.title: A cash-out refinance nets them $15,725 after costs take 32.8% of the equity
slides.side:
New principal and interest at 7.0% for 30 years, down from the original 7.25%: **$2,038 a month**, or $24,457 a year.

That's $820 a year more than today's $23,637. The loan is bigger, and the 30-year clock restarts.
slides.notes:
Now the first funding idea: a cash-out refinance of Cedar Ridge.

They paid $385,000. Value has grown 3% a year, which is an assumption, to $408,446. At 75% loan-to-value the new loan is $306,334. Pay off the $282,951 balance, and the equity removed is $23,383. Then the refinance costs come out. I assumed 2.5% of the new loan, which is $7,658; your written quote replaces that. That leaves $15,725 in cash.

Look at that ratio. Costs take 32.8% of the equity they pulled out. That's what happens when the equity you remove is small.

The new rate is 7.0% for 30 years. That's a bit lower than the original 7.25%, so the payment only goes up $820 a year, to $24,457. That sounds mild. But the loan is bigger, and the 30-year clock starts over. So they're paying down principal more slowly than they were yesterday.

slides.title: After the refinance, the actual year's cash flow falls from -$1,022 to -$1,842

box.label: What the refinance buys
box.text: $15,725 covers about 11% of the $142,688 it took to buy and launch Cedar Ridge.

slides.notes:
Here's the new payment run against three cases.

On the underwritten base, cash flow drops from $5,572 to $4,752. On the original weak case, the bad year they planned for at $265 and 50% occupancy, it's minus $6,295 a year. And on the year they actually had, it's minus $1,842. That's worse than the minus $1,022 before the refinance.

So what does the refinance buy them? $15,725. Cedar Ridge took $142,688 of total cash to get into, counting the down payment, closing costs, and furnishing. The refinance covers about 11% of what a second house would need, and it makes the property they already own a little weaker.

That's the trade. Some cash now, a bigger loan for the next 30 years. Always run the new payment against your weak case and your actual year, not only the base case you hoped for.

slides.title: A HELOC on their $520,000 home could open a line of up to $156,000
slides.side: They draw $100,000 (assumption). Interest-only costs **$667 a month at 8.0%** and **$833 at 10.0%**.

side_box.label: Stress test
side_box.text: A 10% drop to $468,000 cuts the limit to $374,400. They owe $260,000 + $100,000 = $360,000 (76.9%). Room left falls from $56,000 to $14,400, and the drop itself can trigger a freeze.

slides.notes:
The second idea is a line of credit on the house they live in. It's worth $520,000 with a $260,000 mortgage.

Suppose a lender allows a combined loan-to-value of 80%. That's your mortgage plus the line, as a share of the home's value. That's an assumption; the lender sets the real limit. 80% of $520,000 is $416,000 of total debt. Subtract the mortgage, and the line could go up to $156,000.

Say they draw $100,000 toward property two. I priced it at 8% and 10%, both assumptions. Interest-only during the draw costs $8,000 or $10,000 a year. Once a 20-year repayment starts, it's $836 or $965 a month.

Now the stress test. If their home drops 10% to $468,000, the 80% limit falls to $374,400. They'd owe $360,000, which is 76.9%. That's still under 80%, but the room left falls from $56,000 to $14,400. And the CFPB lists a significant value drop itself as a reason a lender may freeze the line.

slides.title: Borrowing the down payment turns property two's thin base case negative
slides.text: Property two is a Cedar Ridge twin with the same price and DSCR terms (assumption). Base cash flow $5,572. Original weak case -$5,475.
columns: Property two cash flow after HELOC interest

box.label: What's at stake
box.text: The weak case becomes a five-figure gap every year, and their own home secures part of the money.

slides.notes:
Now put that HELOC cost on a second house.

Suppose property two is a Cedar Ridge twin with the same DSCR terms. Its base cash flow is $5,572 and its weak case is minus $5,475, straight from the original plan. The HELOC is a household bill, but I charge it to property two because property two is why they borrowed. Subtract the interest.

At 8%, the base case becomes minus $2,428. At 10%, it's minus $4,428. The weak case turns into minus $13,475 or minus $15,475 a year.

A base case that was thin goes negative once the down payment is borrowed. And the weak case is a five-figure gap every year, with the house they live in securing part of the money.

That's why you price the stress rate. A HELOC rate is usually variable, so the payment can change from month to month. If the plan only works at today's rate, it doesn't work.

slides.title: After a HELOC-funded twin, savings fall $43,900.50 short of their reserve rule
slides.side:
**PITIA** is principal, interest, property tax, insurance, and association dues. Cedar Ridge has no HOA. Six months is $2,557 × 6 = $15,342 per house.

Needed: $30,684 + $51,000 = **$81,684**, none borrowed.

side_box.label: Kept simple
side_box.text: We hold $80,471.50 flat. In your worksheet, use today's actual balance.

slides.notes:
Before the scorecard, here's the test that decides this case: cash reserves.

After buying and launching Cedar Ridge, Maya and Chris had $80,471.50 left. PA.12 walks through each step. I hold that number flat to keep the example simple. In your own worksheet, use today's balance, after any shortfalls you covered.

A twin costs $142,688 all in. I test the HELOC route, because savings alone can't cover that and the refinance only yields $15,725. With $100,000 from the HELOC, savings supply $42,688. That leaves $37,783.50.

Now what they need. PITIA is principal, interest, property tax, insurance, and association dues. Cedar Ridge has no HOA. Six months of PITIA on two houses is $30,684. Add the $51,000 emergency fund, and they need $81,684, none of it borrowed. They're short by $43,900.50.

Adding the refinance cash would leave $53,508.50. That's still short, and it raises Cedar Ridge's payment.

slides.title: Cedar Ridge fails four of the five tests Maya and Chris wrote, so the answer is not yet
rows: Cash flow of $0 or more, no top-ups
6 months PITIA (loan payment + tax + insurance) per property, plus emergency fund, none borrowed
Property two weak case at stress rate
Covered by W-2 income for 12 months, no new debt
Named backup for every OP.7 role

bands.d: Every test passes. Move to a property-two buy box (PA.1).
Any test fails and the No rule doesn't apply. A No in rows 1-3 always means at least not yet.
Property one fails even its base case, or the household can't carry the weak case.

slides.notes:
Here's the pass rule Maya and Chris wrote before they looked at a single listing. The thresholds are their choices. They aren't industry standards.

Test one: trailing NOI at 90% or more of the base case. They're at 77.4%. No. Test two: property one covers its own debt without top-ups. It's at minus $1,022. No. Test three: reserves. We just saw they're $43,900.50 short. No.

Test four depends on their household budget, so it isn't scored. And minus $15,475 is the interest-only number. Once repayment starts at 10%, the gap grows to about minus $17,055. Test five: one cleaner, no backup. No.

Now read the bands. Check the No rule first. Cedar Ridge's base case covers its loan, and the household test is open, so it isn't No. Four tests fail, so the answer is not yet. A No in the first three rows always means at least not yet. Those rows describe property one and your cash.

slides.title: Not yet comes with a fix list and a date to rerun the worksheet
items: Find why rate and occupancy slipped, using the tools from Sam's OP.5 lesson.
Confirm the water heater was a one-off repair.
Hire a backup cleaner.
Rerun the worksheet after the next 90-day review.

box.label: Notice what did not drive the answer
box.text: The refinance and the HELOC were both available. Borrowing capacity is not the same as a reason to borrow.

slides.notes:
Not yet isn't a vague answer. It comes with specific next steps and a date.

Maya and Chris find out why the rate and occupancy slipped. The pricing tools from Sam's OP.5 lesson are where they start. They confirm the water heater really was a one-off and not the first of several repairs. They hire a backup cleaner. Then they rerun this whole worksheet after their next 90-day review.

They don't need a new property right now. They need a better year from the one they have.

Notice what did not drive the answer. The refinance was available. The HELOC was available. The money was there. Borrowing capacity is not the same as a reason to borrow, and that's the habit I want you to build.

[Recording note: Preston can add a real example here if he has one.]

slides.title: Write your pass rule before you look at a single listing
slides.text: Use the trailing 12 months ending last month. Date every source. Check the No rule first; a No in rows 1-3 means at least not yet.
rows: Property one cash flow without top-ups
Cash reserves after purchase, excluding undrawn credit
Property two weak case, financing at stress rate
Market: the risk you accept, one stop condition
Team: primary and backup for each OP.7 role, both houses
Systems: a named setup for both houses
slides.notes:
Now it's your turn. The full worksheet has three parts.

Part A is your trailing 12 against your underwriting, with a source, a date, and a one-line cause on every row. Part B puts your funding options side by side: savings only, a cash-out refinance, and a HELOC. For each, write the net cash, the new payment at today's rate and at a stress rate, and what's at risk as collateral. Savings put no new collateral at risk.

This slide is Part C, the pass rule. It has seven rows. Maya and Chris used five; market choice and systems are the extra two. Write your thresholds before you look at listings. If you write them after you've fallen for a house, they'll bend.

Then fill in your results and circle one decision. Proceed to a property-two buy box in PA.1. Not yet, with a recheck date. Or no, and hold one property. Date it, and have each owner sign it. That signature makes the thresholds harder to move later.
slides.caption: Market choice: write the risk you accept and one condition that would stop you. Systems: a named setup for both houses.

slides.title: Your CPA, lenders, insurer, and licensing office each confirm a different piece
rows: The trailing 12 matches the books and bank records; repairs vs improvements are classified correctly
Appraised value, max LTV for an STR, coverage ratio definition, rate, points (upfront fees to lower the rate), costs, reserves, prepayment penalty on the current loan
Max CLTV, draw and repayment periods, index and margin, rate caps, minimum payment, fees, freeze or reduce conditions
How HELOC or refinance interest is treated (Pub 936 and use of proceeds); how property two affects depreciation and losses (SR.3)
Property two's exact address permits the planned use (SR.1)
STR coverage for property two; whether a combined policy changes deductibles or terms
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what.

Your bookkeeper or CPA confirms the trailing 12 matches the books and the bank, and that repairs and improvements are classified correctly.

The refinance lender confirms, in writing, the appraised value, the maximum loan-to-value for a short-term rental, and how they define the coverage ratio. Get the rate, points, which are upfront fees to lower the rate, costs, reserves, and any prepayment penalty on your current loan too.

The HELOC lender's plan disclosures tell you the limit, the draw and repayment periods, and the index and margin. They also show the minimum payment and the conditions that let them freeze or reduce the line.

Your CPA answers the interest question from Publication 936, and how a second property affects your depreciation and loss position. Resource SR.3 helps with that conversation.

The licensing office or an STR attorney checks property two's exact address. And your insurer confirms the house can be covered for short-term rental use.

items: Export 12 months of platform earnings and the property's bank and card statements.
Fill Part A: underwriting, trailing 12, variance, and a one-line cause per row.
Write your pass-rule thresholds in Part C and date them before you browse listings.
Ask one lender for a written refinance or HELOC quote, with its freeze terms.
slides.next: Next: **OP.12 Exit Strategy** takes Cedar Ridge to year 5. Bring your trailing-12 report.
slides.title: Four steps this week turn property one's records into a dated answer
slides.notes:
Four things to do this week.

Pull the last 12 months of platform earnings and the property's bank and card statements. Fill in Part A of the worksheet, with a one-line cause for every variance. Write your pass-rule thresholds in Part C, and date them before you browse anything. And ask one lender for a written refinance or HELOC quote. Make sure it includes the terms that let them freeze or cut a line.

Next up is OP.12, Exit Strategy: Hold, Refinance, Sell, or 1031 Exchange. Scaling is one way to change the investment. The other ways are to refinance and keep one property, to sell, or to exchange into something different.

OP.12 takes the same Cedar Ridge numbers to year 5. Bring your trailing-12 report with you. It becomes the starting point for your hold-or-exit worksheet.

slides.title: The HELOC and home-equity interest rules here come from CFPB and IRS pages

items.title: CFPB: What is a home equity line of credit (HELOC)?
items.note: Draw period (10-year example), minimum payments, variable rate on a public index, required disclosures

items.title: CFPB: What you should know about HELOCs (brochure)
items.note: Repayment over time or all at once when the draw ends

items.title: CFPB: What you should know about home equity lines of credit (booklet)
items.note: Freeze or reduce on a value decline or material change in finances; risk of losing the home

items.title: IRS Publication 936
items.note: Home equity interest deductible as mortgage interest only if proceeds buy, build, or improve the home

items.title: Fannie Mae Selling Guide B3-4.1-01, Minimum Reserve Requirements
items.note: Reserves can be required beyond the down payment

items.title: Airbnb: co-host permissions
items.note: Permission levels; the listing owner is responsible for co-hosts

slides.notes:
These are the sources behind this lesson.

The three CFPB pages cover how a HELOC works. That's the draw and repayment periods, the variable rate tied to an index, and the disclosures the lender must give you. They also cover when a lender can freeze or reduce the line. IRS Publication 936 covers the limit on deducting home equity interest as mortgage interest.

The CFPB Loan Estimate guide is how you compare written refinance quotes. Fannie Mae's reserve rules show that a lender can require reserves on top of the down payment. Airbnb's help page covers co-host permission levels.

The Cedar Ridge numbers come from our recurring example file, cases B1, B2, B4, and B7. The trailing-12, HELOC, and pass-rule figures are new assumptions I built for teaching.

Check each rule against the current source before you rely on it. Lender terms and plan disclosures vary, so your own written quotes come first.
